r-h2o.name: H2O Extreme
r-h2o.teaser: Kiting off Galu since 2003, on the lagoon it moved south to find
r-h2o.story: The south coast's longest-running kite school, IKO-affiliated, now teaches from Blue Marlin on Galu. It left mid-strip, in its own words, because down here the water is clearer, the beach wider and the riding better. Its wind page sets the calendar the whole beach lives by: kaskazi from mid-December to mid-March, 15 to 20 knots filling in around 10:30; kusi from June to mid-September, 18 to 22 knots, cooler and gustier. Inside the reef the lagoon holds waist-deep flat water at every tide. Wingfoil, windsurf, SUP and kayaks are for rent too.
r-h2o.why: Come inside one of the two wind windows; outside them there is nothing to teach.
facts: Blue Marlin Beach Hotel, Galu; daily 09:00–18:00, lessons once the wind fills
Kaskazi mid-December to mid-March (15–20 knots); kusi June to mid-September (18–22 knots)
3-day beginner course EUR 400 a head, two students to one instructor (IKO listing, Oct 2026); other rates by WhatsApp
By WhatsApp, ahead in either wind season
A kaskazi morning, when the breeze fills in around 10:30

sources.label: IKO school listing, H2O Extreme Diani

r-kite254.name: Kite254
r-kite254.teaser: The coach's voice in your helmet while the kite is still in the air, out on the southern flat
r-kite254.story: Two bases: Pallet Cafe on the quiet southern stretch of Galu, and Diani Sea Lodge. Lessons run on current Ozone kites, and each student wears a radio helmet, so the instructor on the beach talks you through the turn while you are still in it instead of explaining it afterwards on the sand. The school's own spot guide is frank about why Diani works: a reef-protected, waist-deep lagoon and roughly six months of trade wind spread across the two monsoons. When the season allows it runs downwinders and kite day-trips south toward Funzi.
r-kite254.why: Ask for the downwinder toward Funzi once you can hold an edge.
facts: Pallet Cafe, southern Galu, and Diani Sea Lodge; daily 10:00–18:00
The two trade-wind windows, about six months a year
3-hour taster USD 130 semi-private, USD 210 private (seen Aug 2026); course prices in the craft section
A downwinder toward Funzi, when the season allows

r-crab.name: Diving the Crab
r-crab.teaser: The dive house that put a ship on the seabed: the Funguo, upright on the sand off Diani
r-crab.story: Taking divers out since 1985 from the Nomad beach, with around twenty-nine sites inside a forty-minute boat ride. Its signature site is one it made: the shop re-sank the MV Alpha Funguo off Diani as an artificial reef, and she sits upright on sand at about 30 m, deck and holds intact. Barracuda and trevally school over the hull; morays and frogfish keep to the shadows below. It is Advanced Open Water depth, run almost daily in season. From October to March the sea lies calm and visibility often reaches 30 m; in the kusi months the chop cuts it down and the shops teach instead.
r-crab.why: Take the two-tank morning boat to the Funguo in the calm months; dolphins often ride the bow on the way.
facts: October to March, visibility often to 30 m; June to September the kusi cuts it
On request; no published rates (seen Aug 2026)
Phone +254 723 108 108, the day before in season
The Alpha Funguo wreck, for Advanced Open Water divers

sources.label: PADI dive-centre listing, Diving the Crab

r-ocean-tribe.name: Ocean Tribe Scuba
r-ocean-tribe.teaser: The younger shop: ten sites in a half-hour ride and a 2026 price list anyone can check
r-ocean-tribe.story: Based at The 41 Beach Club, with a booking office at Baobab Beach Resort. Its ten local sites run from Tiwi Wall and Kisima Mungu to Galu, Mwanamoji and the Funguo wreck, all within about thirty minutes, and it runs full-day dhow trips down to Kisite. What sets it apart on this strip is paperwork: a current price-list PDF and an instructor calendar on its own site, which is rare and checkable. Its pages are honest in the other direction too: its whale-shark trips are not running for the 2025/26 season.
r-ocean-tribe.why: Pair Tiwi Wall with the Funguo on one morning.
facts: The 41 Beach Club, Diani; booking office at Baobab Beach Resort
2026 price list published as a PDF on its site (seen Aug 2026)
Our August 2026 check found an SSI shop that runs crossover courses for PADI divers; a booking listing seen in October 2026 calls it a PADI 5 Star IDC centre. Ask which card you will be issued

r-skydive.name: Skydive Swahili
r-skydive.teaser: Forty seconds of freefall over the reef stripes, then a sand landing in front of Blue Marlin
r-skydive.story: A KCAA-licensed tandem operation, affiliated to the USPA and UPT, jumping year-round from Galu. The day runs as a scenic climb over the lagoon, about forty seconds of freefall, a canopy ride over water striped turquoise and brown by the reef, and a landing on the sand in front of the hotel. The fact that matters for a crew day off is the calendar: it flies Thursday to Monday and is shut on Tuesday and Wednesday. If the wind has cancelled the kite lesson, this is the other way to see the lagoon.
r-skydive.why: Go on a dry-season morning, when the reef colours are clearest from altitude.
facts: Blue Marlin Beach Hotel, Galu; Thursday to Monday 08:00–18:00
Year-round; December to March mornings for the clearest colours
Tandem USD 350, photo and video package USD 100 extra (seen Aug 2026)
Online or WhatsApp +254 717 907 907; never on a Tuesday or Wednesday
The canopy ride down over the lagoon

r-fishing.name: Diani Fishing Club
r-fishing.teaser: Three named boats to the Pemba Channel drop-offs, billfish released, the season booked not wished
r-fishing.story: Princess Layla, Shuwari and White Dove work the Pemba Channel and the Shimoni drop-offs for blue, black and striped marlin, sailfish, wahoo, dorado and tuna, under a stated tag-and-release policy for billfish. Its feed showed tournaments through March 2025 and a 785 lb blue marlin in December 2024. Billfish peak from October to April on the north-flowing current; a July day off should not expect sailfish, though the kusi months are the time for yellowfin and giant trevally. The site hides its phone number, so bookings go through its form.
r-fishing.why: Book the billfish months well ahead; take what the kusi gives the rest of the year.
facts: Diani central; charters leave early morning
Billfish October to April; yellowfin and giant trevally August to October
By the form on its site, well ahead for December to February
A December sailfish on light tackle, released

The club's news called the December 2024 fish a Kenya record; Kenya's books already hold blue marlin past 1,000 lb, including a 1,062 lb fish off Watamu in March 2014, so read it as a club or line-class mark at most

r-whales.name: Whale Shark Adventures
r-whales.teaser: Two hours with a hydrophone over the side and humpback song coming up through the hull
r-whales.story: Run by Volker Bassen, who founded the East African Whale Shark Trust. When the humpbacks pass on their migration from Antarctic water, from early July with the peak from early August to mid-October, it runs two-hour trips with a hydrophone lowered over the side so you hear the song before you see a blow. It also flies spotter-plane whale-shark expeditions in the windows it gives as February to March and mid-August to December. Sightings are genuinely hit and miss, and any operator selling a guarantee is not telling the truth. Sold as a search, it is a fine one.
r-whales.why: Go for the sound: the hydrophone is what this boat has that the others do not.
facts: Diani central; every trip depends on the sea state
Humpbacks early July to mid-October, peak from early August
WhatsApp +254 720 555 222; reconfirm, its blog trail is years old

Whale-shark season: this operator gives February to March and mid-August to December, Diving the Crab lists November to February, other Diani sellers say October to March, and a 2018 report put the peak at 1 February to 15 March

sources.label: ATC News, whale-shark migration off Diani (2018)

s-no-nails.name: The ship with no nails
s-no-nails.teaser: Two thousand years of sewn hulls, then the nailed jahazi won, and its heirs still sail from Shimoni
s-no-nails.story: The oldest sailing directions for this coast, the Greek Periplus of the Erythraean Sea of the first century AD, describe 'sewed boats' at the market town of Rhapta. In 1498 Vasco da Gama's chronicler logged the same ship: 'There are no nails, and the planks are held together by cords... The sails are made of palm-matting.' That was the mtepe, pegged and sewn with coir rolled from coconut husk. It lasted so long that James Hornell wrote its obituary in the Mariner's Mirror in 1941. The nailed jahazi, from the Persian jahāz, ship, replaced it because, as a 2023 study of Lamu's boatbuilding village Matondoni puts it, the trade 'needed a stronger vessel'. Marion Kaplan rode the last of the ocean dhow trade in 1974 for National Geographic. The hulls lived on by changing cargo: Monsoon, built at Shimoni by Shirazi shipwrights, now carries day-trippers beside Almasi, launched 2014.
s-no-nails.why: ★ The old hand's point: stitches clamp the planks at hundreds of points and let the hull flex, so a sewn ship survives drying coral landings that spring a nailed hull's fastenings; and a wooden working boat survives by changing its cargo, never itself.
facts: The mtepe models in the Fort Jesus museum, Mombasa; then board Monsoon or Almasi at Shimoni on the dhow day (Pilli Pipa sails both)

s-ngalawa.name: The ngalawa's outriggers
s-ngalawa.teaser: The canoe on your beach carries a rig idea that crossed from Indonesia by way of Madagascar
s-ngalawa.story: The little double-outrigger working the Diani–Chale lagoon has the most far-fetched pedigree of any boat on this sand. The fisheries ethnographer James Hornell set out the classic case in 1919: the double outrigger is Austronesian technology, at home from Indonesia to the Pacific, and it reached East Africa with the same seaborne movement that made Madagascar a Malagasy-speaking island. The hull is narrow, the floats are lashed on, and the whole boat draws a few centimetres. Watch one come in over the reef flat at first light and you are looking at an idea that crossed an ocean. The deeper lesson is that this ocean was a highway, not a barrier.
s-ngalawa.why: ★ The old hand's point: an outrigger is a lever, not a keel; the windward float flies, the leeward float skims, and a hull too narrow to carry a sail becomes a stable platform drawing centimetres, exactly what a fringing-reef coast demands.
facts: First light off Diani or Galu: ask a fisher to show you the pito lashings, still cordage, not bolts

Modern scholarship supports Hornell's Madagascar link, but the route and the date are still argued; A.H.J. Prins titled his 1959 paper on it 'Uncertainties in Coastal Cultural History', and the argument has outlived a century

s-wearing.name: Wearing round
s-wearing.teaser: Why a dhow turns her stern through the wind, and what that one manoeuvre says about a whole ocean
s-wearing.story: The rig on the Wasini channel is technically a settee: a lateen with the front corner cut off, a form already carved on a second-century gravestone. Its price is paid at every change of board. The sail sits to one side of the mast, so on one tack the mast presses into the canvas, the documented 'bad tack'. To tack properly the crew must peak the long yard upright and carry it bodily round the mast. So dhow crews prefer to wear round, turning the stern through the wind, where the wind helps swing the yard instead of fighting it. Read the culture from that: long offshore legs, harbours chosen so you rarely beat, and passages timed to a fair monsoon so the boat almost never fights the wind at all.
s-wearing.why: ★ The old hand's point: watching a dhow put about is watching risk management; wearing gives up ground to leeward but keeps that enormous yard under control.
facts: From the bow of a Shimoni dhow, watch the channel traffic change board and count which boats tack and which wear

s-pilot.name: The Pilot of Malindi
s-pilot.teaser: Did the great Ahmad ibn Majid pilot da Gama? The scholars say no, and the truth is better
s-pilot.story: Ahmad ibn Majid, born at Julfar around the 1430s, was the greatest of the ocean's mu'allims, master navigators, author of the Kitab al-Fawa'id: star rhumbs, monsoon timings, port latitudes. The record of 1498 is plain enough. Turned away at Mombasa, welcomed at Malindi, da Gama sailed on 24 April with a pilot the sultan supplied and crossed in 23 days on the first of the south-west monsoon. Going home against the calendar took over ninety days and roughly half his crews, and he burned the São Rafael off this coast for want of men. Offshore the tool was the kamal, a wooden card on a knotted string held in the teeth, measuring latitude in finger-widths of about 1°36'. But stars only find the coast. To thread the reef, the 1889 Africa Pilot says, bring the Wasini peaks 'their own breadth open of Rashid point', past two islets named Kisite and Mpunguti, as they still are.
s-pilot.why: ★ The old hand's point: on this ocean the departure date was the navigation, and celestial latitude only finds the coast; steep-to coral gives the lead no warning, so you thread it by marks in line and water colour, which GPS still cannot do for you.
facts: On the dhow out of Shimoni, watch the captain take the reef by eye past Kisite and Mpunguti; in Mombasa, the seaward ramparts of Fort Jesus overlook the harbour mouth where da Gama was turned away, a century before the fort

The legend that ibn Majid piloted da Gama rests on a Meccan chronicle written about eighty years later, which adds that he was drunk; the eyewitness accounts call the pilot a Gujarati, ibn Majid was by then near seventy and writing of his seafaring as done, and modern scholarship rejects the identification

s-round-trip.name: One round trip a year
s-round-trip.teaser: Kaskazi out, kusi home, and the months in between that made the Swahili world
s-round-trip.story: The 1889 Admiralty Africa Pilot sets the calendar precisely: the north-east monsoon reaches this coast in mid-to-late November through a fortnight of calms and squalls; the south-west arrives around March and blows full force from June to September. A nahodha who ran down from the Gulf in December could not sail home until the kusi set in. So he stayed for months, selling dates and salt fish, loading ivory and boriti mangrove poles cut in bays like Gazi for the treeless Gulf, and taking wives. That wintering-over is the intermarriage, and the Swahili language and towns are its sediment. The Pilot logs the coastal current off this reef at one knot with you in kaskazi and three against you in kusi, and says the inshore channel behind Wasini was worth taking because 'all current is thereby avoided.'
s-round-trip.why: ★ The old hand's point: the monsoon was a calendar, not a forecast; one round trip a year meant the port stay was the business model, not dead time, and the south coast's towns exist because captains had to stay.
facts: Gazi Bay's mangroves were boriti cutting grounds; today the community project Mikoko Pamoja manages 117 hectares of them for carbon credits. The ngalawa off Galu still sail the same seasonal wind

s-1331.name: One night in Mombasa, 1331
s-1331.teaser: The first eyewitness of this coast found island cities that trusted the monsoon with their bread
s-1331.story: Coming down from Mogadishu on a monsoon ship in 1331, Ibn Battuta left the earliest surviving eyewitness account of Mombasa: an island with fruit trees but no cereals, its grain brought in by sea, its people living 'chiefly of bananas and fish', 'pious, honourable, and upright', their wooden mosques well built. He stayed one night and sailed on for Kilwa, which he found 'very fine and substantially built'. The portrait he leaves is a string of rich Muslim island cities provisioned entirely by dhow and fully networked into the Indian Ocean a century and a half before the Portuguese arrived. The port lunch was bananas and fish because that is what an island with fruit trees and a reef produces; provisioning by sea is the oldest local trade a visiting ship joins.
s-1331.why: ★ The old hand's point: an island city that imports its grain trusts the monsoon absolutely; Mombasa's food security in 1331 was a shipping schedule.
facts: Mombasa Old Town stands on the town he slept in; on Diani's own shore, the Kongo Mosque is the south coast's surviving piece of that mosque-building coast
He calls Kilwa's buildings wood, yet the excavated Kilwa of exactly that period is coral stone; scholars still argue over what he saw or how he wrote it up

s-galleot.name: One galleot against a coast
s-galleot.teaser: Mir Ali Beg turned the whole coast with eighty men, and Fort Jesus is the receipt
s-galleot.story: In 1585–86 the Ottoman corsair Mir Ali Beg came down this coast with a single galleot and about eighty men, and sailed home having taken the allegiance of every major Swahili port but Malindi, three laden Portuguese ships, a gathered fleet of some 24 vessels and roughly 150,000 cruzados. He came back in 1588–89 with five galleots. Goa had learned: Tomé de Sousa Coutinho sealed Mombasa harbour with eighteen ships and burned the Turkish flotilla. Then the land intervened, and the corsair's men were destroyed between the mainland and the guns. What nobody disputes is the consequence: shaken by how cheaply one corsair had turned a coastline, Portugal built Fort Jesus in 1593–96.
s-galleot.why: ★ The old hand's point: on a monsoon coast sea power is timing plus legitimacy, not tonnage, and a victor's chronicle should be read like a log kept by an interested party, because its numbers are weapons too.
facts: Fort Jesus, Mombasa, is the corsair's monument, built expressly against the Ottomans after these raids

The Portuguese chronicles say thousands of Zimba, a people they called cannibals, fell on Mombasa from the mainland and finished Ali Beg's men; historians treat the Zimba story and its numbers with open scepticism

s-siege.name: Thirty-three months
s-siege.teaser: The siege that ended Portuguese Mombasa was decided at sea, by seven days and a sunken frigate
s-siege.story: On 13 March 1696 the fleet of Saif bin Sultan, Imam of Oman, shut between fifty and seventy Portuguese soldiers and several hundred African and Swahili defenders inside Fort Jesus. It was decided on the water. Queen Fatuma of Zanzibar sent three dhows of supplies, captured and burned. Relief squadrons from Goa broke through three times; one frigate, the Santo António de Tanná, was lost under the walls in 1697. By December 1698 the garrison was the captain, nine men and a priest. The fort fell on 13 December; a Portuguese relief fleet sighted Mombasa on the 20th, seven days late. From 1977 to 1980 the Institute of Nautical Archaeology and the National Museums of Kenya excavated the frigate from a barge in the working harbour: African and Indian pottery, Chinese porcelain, and ordnance lighter than a ship of her size and purpose should have carried.
s-siege.why: ★ The old hand's point: a fortress on an island is a ship at permanent anchor and lives exactly as long as its sea lifeline; a ship tied to it has no sea room, and you can read an empire's exhaustion in her armament list.
facts: Walk the seaward rampart of Fort Jesus, then find the frigate's pottery, porcelain and two bronze cannons in the museum, metres from where she lies

sources.label: Institute of Nautical Archaeology, Santo António de Tanná excavation

s-chasers.name: The dhow chasers
s-chasers.teaser: Open boats against the slave trade, in exactly the water your dhow day crosses
s-chasers.story: From 1874 the Royal Navy kept HMS London, an old two-decker turned depot ship, moored at Zanzibar to suppress the Indian Ocean slave trade, and the real work fell to her small boats: 39 slave dhows taken in these channels in eighteen months of 1874–76. The cost showed on 3 December 1881 off Pemba. Captain Charles Brownrigg took the pinnace alongside a dhow flying French colours to inspect her papers; armed men rose from cover, and he and four of his crew were killed. The dhow beat off the pinnace and got away. The frank first-hand account of the work is G.L. Sulivan's Dhow Chasing in Zanzibar Waters (1873), open about how often the trade slipped through. These channels rewarded shallow draft, local knowledge and the land breeze, and the dhow skippers held all three.
s-chasers.why: ★ The old hand's point: the fighting unit was an open boat boarding over a low gunwale, where rank protected nobody, and the arithmetic stays honest: 39 dhows in a trade of thousands; patrols raised the price of slaving, and treaties and the 1873 closure of Zanzibar's market did the rest.
facts: The patrol ground is the water between Shimoni and the Kisite reefs; ashore, the Shimoni caves hold the trade's shore story

Our older notes had Lloyd Mathews hunting the slaver down at Wete and taking him mortally wounded; the 1881 Admiralty and press accounts say only that the dhow escaped, and Mathews had by then left the navy's boats to command the Sultan's army

sources.label: Royal Museums Greenwich memorials, Captain C.J. Brownrigg
Papers Past, 'An encounter with a slaver' (Dec 1881)

s-bamvua.name: Bamvua and msindizo
s-bamvua.teaser: The Diani–Chale fishery runs on the moon twice over, and the month is opened by radio from Zanzibar
s-bamvua.story: Researchers who counted every landing from Diani to Gazi in 2003–06 wrote down the calendar the fishers actually keep. The lunar month opens with the first sighting of the waxing crescent, coordinated, remarkably, by a daily radio broadcast from Zanzibar. The spring tides around new and full moon are bamvua, the prime fishing days; the neaps are msindizo, 'to rest', when trap fishers stay ashore rather than set gear in the dark of a late low. The fishers even corrected the scientists' grid: Diani's lagoon is shallower than Chale's, so one afternoon can be resting water at Chale and bamvua at Mwaepe. Over a year the clock adds up to roughly 570 fishers, 85,551 fisher-days and about 403 tonnes of fish.
s-bamvua.why: ★ The old hand's point: the moon makes the tide and the sighted crescent makes the month, so religion and hydrography agree on which mornings a canoe goes out; ask a captain 'bamvua au msindizo?' and a chef learns which dawns the auction is worth the walk.
facts: Any landing at first light, Mwaepe the nearest to the Galu hotels: on a bamvua day the sand crowds with ngalawa, on msindizo it is nearly empty

s-kuchukua.name: Kuchukua, the women's fishery
s-kuchukua.teaser: The women of the flats do not call themselves fishers, and land half of what this coast eats at home
s-kuchukua.story: A 2021–23 survey of 141 fishers in the Shimoni–Vanga seascape mapped a sea divided by gender: men beyond the reef crest with handlines and basket traps, women on the seagrass flats on foot, gathering by hand and hunting octopus with a pointed stick. The women call the work kuchukua, 'to take', and do not call themselves wavuvi, fishers; every man interviewed did. Octopus comes only in the bamvua windows, eight days twice a month, yet their catch supplies about half the seafood eaten at home. At Munje, between Diani and Msambweni, the Beach Management Unit closed 4,000 m² of flat to octopus in mid-2023; Salim Juma Shee opposed it and became a monitor. Reopened for three days that October, it gave about 650 kg. The supporting NGO admits its first closure failed for lack of sensitisation.
s-kuchukua.why: ★ The old hand's point: half the protein here is caught on legs, not hulls, on an eight-day spring-tide lock; rest a flat like a field for three or four months and harvest on the big low, and restraint out-fishes the daily speargun.
facts: At spring low from Diani to Wasini, the lines of women crossing the flats with buckets and sticks are the fishery working; a Munje opening day, every three to four months, is the best moment on this coast to buy pweza by the hundredweight

s-said-no.name: The landings that said no
s-said-no.teaser: Two Diani beaches kept the pull seines off by tradition alone, and out-fished their neighbours
s-said-no.story: A 1997 study of the Diani–Chale area recorded one of the oldest and most elaborate traditions of sacred sea sites on the Kenyan coast: spirit places fishers hesitated even to name, offerings at annual ceremonies, a sea peopled by the playful kibwengo and the drowning kitunusi. The customs were never fisheries management; their purpose, the paper is careful to say, was to appease spirits, not to regulate stocks. And yet two Diani landings, Mvuleni and Mwanyaza, kept the destructive pull seines off their beaches for more than twenty years by argument from tradition alone, while neighbouring landings took up the gear. The measurements came out on the elders' side, with higher catches per fisher at the two beaches that refused. Today's Beach Management Units are the legal descendants of that authority.
s-said-no.why: ★ The old hand's point: customary authority measurably protected livelihoods though conservation was never its aim; a sailor knows the mechanism, port discipline enforced by respect rather than regulation, working exactly as far as respect reached.
facts: Mvuleni and Mwanyaza are still working landing beaches a short walk from the hotels; buy your fish there and you stand in the story

x-crab-course.name: The dive ladder at Diving the Crab
x-crab-course.teaser: Start never having breathed underwater and, if you keep coming back, end up qualified to teach
x-crab-course.story: This is the one, for three plain reasons. It is a PADI 5 Star IDC Resort, the tier that trains new instructors, not merely new divers, so the whole ladder from first breath to teaching card sits under one roof, on one reef. The door is open: anyone can enrol, and the first lessons run in the shop's own training pool before the sea. And the house has staying power: it has worked this coast since 1985, with six instructors and Nitrox on site. One honest gap: no instructor is named on its public pages, so ask for a name when you book.
x-crab-course.why: Book the course, not a single dive: the point here is the ladder.
facts: PADI courses from a first pool session to Open Water and beyond, up to the instructor development course
On request; no published course prices (seen Aug 2026)
Ahead, by phone +254 723 108 108 or through its site; the sea sites are told in the reef section

sources.label: PADI dive-centre listing, Diving the Crab

x-kite254.name: The two kite schools
x-kite254.teaser: Radio helmets at one, two decades of seniority at the other, and neither tells you who will teach you
x-kite254.story: Both schools are IKO-affiliated, so the certificate is a real one, and both teach in the waist-deep lagoon where a beginner can stand up and start again. Kite254 is the course to pick if you learn by ear: radio-helmet coaching means the fix reaches you mid-mistake, the kit is recent Ozone, and its prices are published. H2O Extreme has taught here since 2003 and moved to Galu to teach on better water, which tells you how seriously it takes the lesson. What neither publishes is a teacher's name, so you meet your instructor on the sand.
x-kite254.why: Pick Kite254 if you want the coaching in your ear, H2O Extreme if you want the longest record on this beach.
facts: An IKO beginner course: kite control on the beach, body-dragging in the lagoon, then first rides on the board
Kite254: 3-hour taster, 3-day intro or 4-day full course. H2O Extreme: 3-day beginner course of three 3-hour sessions
Kite254: 3-day intro USD 375 (two students to one instructor), 4-day course USD 480–720, gear included (seen Aug 2026). H2O Extreme: 3-day course EUR 400 a head, two to one (IKO listing, Oct 2026)
Kite254 by WhatsApp +254 719 891 835; H2O Extreme by WhatsApp through its site
A named teacher: neither school publishes who will instruct you

sources.label: IKO school listing, H2O Extreme Diani

x-akamba.name: Akamba Handicraft Co-operative
x-akamba.teaser: Since 1963, about 2,800 carvers by hand, and 70 to 80 per cent of each sale to the maker
x-akamba.story: Founded in 1963 by about a hundred Kamba carvers who brought the Wamunyu tradition to Mombasa, the co-operative now counts roughly 2,800 members working rosewood, ebony and neem with axe and chisel, no machines. You walk the open sheds and follow a piece from the choice of log through rough carving, detailing and finishing, then buy from the co-op store, where seventy to eighty per cent of the price goes to the carver, against a fraction of that on the beach. Most of the carvings on Diani's stalls were cut here or in Wamunyu and trucked down. The test for real ebony is in the warning below.
x-akamba.why: Pair it with an airport run and buy your carving in the shed it was cut in.
facts: Walk the carving sheds, meet individual carvers, buy at the co-op store
A weekday morning, when the sheds are fullest; 45 to 60 minutes each way from Diani, ferry-free since the Dongo Kundu bypass
At the store, 70–80% of each sale goes to the carver
Walk in, daytime Monday to Saturday; phone +254 746 233 118 ahead, especially for a group
Classes: you can watch, meet the carvers and buy, but you cannot learn the craft here

x-art-club.name: Diani Art Club
x-art-club.teaser: Jimmy, the resident portrait painter, is the one named working maker on this list
x-art-club.story: A small commercial gallery on the Ukunda–Diani road given over to Kenyan artists, from bold abstracts to Maasai handcraft, as it describes itself, and honest about its scale: it sells safari bookings on the side. The reason to go is the resident portrait painter, Jimmy, who takes commissions by WhatsApp. It also keeps real, seasonally published opening hours, which on this strip is itself a mark of seriousness. Find it by the landmark, opposite the GPS petrol station, because the map apps do not show it.
x-art-club.why: Commission a portrait from Jimmy; that is the reason to stop.
facts: Look at the painting wall; commission a portrait from the resident painter
Monday to Saturday 09:00–18:30; Sundays 10:00–18:30, September to February only
Teaching: it takes commissions, not pupils, so you can meet a named maker but not learn from him

x-kaaribu.name: The Kaaribu street-food walk
x-kaaribu.teaser: A registered company, a fixed route, and a door into rooms you would not walk into alone
x-kaaribu.story: Ninety minutes on foot with Kaaribu Experiences, a registered Kenyan company. You meet at Tsunami Garden Cafe, walk Ukunda's market trading cluster, and eat in a kibandaski: cardamom-coconut porridge, viazi karai, chapati and beans, ugali na sukuma, coconut rice with fish. It finishes with an mnazi tasting in a mangwe, the unsigned palm-wine den that is not a walk-in. For a chef with half a day it is the fastest honest map of the town's food economy, and the only verified way for an outsider into the mangwe.
x-kaaribu.why: Spend it before any restaurant money: Ukunda's food makes sense afterwards.
facts: A guided walk through the market, a kibandaski meal and an mnazi tasting
1.5 hours, year-round; the morning slot is best
A day ahead, on its site or +254 732 905 343

x-not-craft.name: What is sold as craft and is not
x-not-craft.teaser: Most of the black 'ebony' on this beach is lighter wood under shoe polish
x-not-craft.story: Real mpingo, East African blackwood, is heavy and dark all the way through. Most stall 'ebony' on the strip is neither: a lighter wood blackened on the surface. Weigh it in your hand, look at the end grain, and scratch an unseen face to see whether the colour survives. Buy at the Akamba co-op sheds instead, where most of the price reaches the carver, and expect to pay more for a piece that is what it says it is. The same goes for the story: do not believe a line about a grandfather unless you are watching the grandfather.
x-not-craft.why: Weigh the piece before you hear the price: real blackwood is heavy.
facts: Bargain on the beach, where it is expected
Bargain at the co-op or with a named artist
Weight and end grain: real mpingo is heavy and dark to the core
Buy at the Akamba co-op, Changamwe, on an airport run

a-biashara.name: Biashara Street, Mombasa
a-biashara.teaser: Where every kikoi on the beach is bought wholesale, and tailors hem your kanga while you wait
a-biashara.story: The kikois and kangas on Diani's stalls are almost all factory prints bought wholesale on this Mombasa street. Its anchor is Mali ya Abdulla, the Kaderdina Hajee Essak house: founded in 1887, on Biashara Street since 1907, five generations in, and so established that leso patterns carry its name. Rows of tailors hem and stitch on the spot. Kangas sell in pairs, a doti, and each is printed with a proverb, the jina. Those proverbs have teeth, so have a Swahili speaker translate before you give one as a present.
a-biashara.why: Buy a doti with a proverb you actually understand, and have it hemmed on the spot.
facts: Mwembe Tayari end of Mombasa CBD; a half-day from Diani since the bypass
Monday to Saturday business hours (unverified); quieter at Friday midday
Mali ya Abdulla, and the tailors working on the pavement
Kangas in pairs; bargaining is standard, done respectfully

a-kentaste.name: Kentaste, Ukunda
a-kentaste.teaser: The coconut cream on Kenyan shelves is pressed minutes from the beach, from 4,000 farmers' nuts
a-kentaste.story: Founded in 2014 as a Kwale family business, Kentaste presses on the order of 30,000 coconuts a day from more than 4,000 smallholders across Kwale, Kilifi and Mombasa, roughly half of them certified organic or Fairtrade. Out come coconut milk, cream, virgin oil, desiccated coconut, flour, chips and water, exported to three continents. There are no tours; it is a working plant on the Ukunda outskirts. The galley consequence is the point: the local, traceable pantry coconut sits on the supermarket shelves on the strip at source prices, so there is no reason to fly tins in.
a-kentaste.why: Stock the galley's coconut here instead of carrying it from home.
facts: Not to visitors: a working factory, no public tours
The Kentaste label on cream, virgin oil and desiccated coconut

a-bixa.name: Kenya Bixa, Tiwi
a-bixa.teaser: The orange annatto in cheddar, smoked fish and rubs is processed on the Diani side of Kwale
a-bixa.story: The annatto, or achiote, that colours cheddar, smoked fish and spice rubs is processed at Tiwi. Kenya Bixa takes in between 1,000 and 1,400 tonnes of seed a year against a capacity of 3,000, from 7,000 to 10,000 contracted smallholders in Kwale, Kilifi and Lamu; the farm-gate price was KES 95 a kilo (seen Aug 2026). At the turn of July and August 2026 Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe launched a drive to double production because the shortfall is on the farms, not in the plant. Once you know the spiky red pods, you see bixa hedges along the south-coast smallholdings everywhere.
a-bixa.why: Learn the spiky red pod; then buy the seed at a spice stall.
facts: Tiwi, north of Diani; an export works, not an attraction
No tours and no factory shop
Spiky red bixa pods in smallholding hedges along the south coast
Achiote seed at the spice stalls
